The test has 30 environments, 630 demonstration videos and 160 tasks with unusual rules that can only be followed by learning from the context. Rules are given as text or video. Among six top models, the best two, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, succeeded on 82% and 76% of computer runs. On robot runs, they managed only 27% and 26%. GPT-6 Astra answered 98% of robot rule questions correctly but finished just 20% of those tasks. The authors say this shows big gaps between digital and physical settings, and between knowing a rule and acting on it.

items.headline: InstructReplay Helps AI Models Learn New Facts Without Forgetting Skills
items.summary: When you teach a chatbot new facts through fine-tuning (extra training on new data), it often gets worse at other things. Researchers found standard fine-tuning cut scores on instruction-following, reasoning and coding tests by 35 points on average. The models also began giving much shorter answers, at least half as long as before. The team proposes InstructReplay. The original model first answers a set of general instructions. During fine-tuning, the model is then kept close to those saved answers. Tested on three model families and two domains, it cut the average drop on five general benchmarks from 28.1 to 2.4 points. It also kept answer length close to the original, and learned new facts as well as standard fine-tuning. It beat seven other methods in all six settings. The authors say the gain comes from replaying the model's own answers.

items.headline: Small AI Models Learn Agent Skills Without Seeing Teacher's Reasoning
items.summary: Researchers found a way to train small AI models to act like stronger ones, even when the strong model hides its step-by-step thinking. Many top models are closed, so their thinking is not available. The team trained students only on the teacher's actions, leaving the thinking block empty. Oddly, the skill still worked when the student later used its own reasoning. They call this cross-format transfer. On the AppWorld task test, Qwen3-4B rose from 7% to 18%. Adding short summaries of the teacher's reasoning lifted it to 35%. Using GPT-5.6 Luna as teacher, Qwen3-4B went from 7% to 48% on AppWorld and from 3% to 28% on SWE-bench Verified. This could make it cheaper to build capable small agents from closed models.

items.headline: New test checks if AI video reasoning holds up in bad visuals
items.summary: Researchers released GRAPE-Bench, a test for AI models that reason about video when the picture is poor. It mixes synthetic videos with twelve types of added damage, plus real driving footage at night or in rain, snow or fog. Each video comes with three questions, from basic safety-related judgments to hard reasoning puzzles. The team found that model rankings can flip between synthetic and real footage. Overall accuracy also hides weak spots at certain question levels. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on synthetic data raised its real-world accuracy from 76.7% to 81.1%. The authors also show a way to steer a model between safety-focused judgments and harder reasoning. This matters because video AI used in areas like driving must stay reliable when conditions are bad.

items.headline: New Benchmark Tests Whether AI Coding Agents Can Find Bugs on Their Own
items.summary: Researchers released SpecEngineeringBench, a test for AI coding agents. Most older tests tell the agent what to check or where to look. This one does not. The agent must work out what to test from the requirements, write the tests, and use the results to find hidden bugs. It has 100 cases from 78 open-source Python projects, each with several known bugs. Seven top coding agents were tested. Their tests usually ran fine, with a 91.47% pass rate on the fixed code, but only 26.36% of tests caught the bugs. Pinpointing the bug also got harder in finer detail: recall fell from 78.11% for files to 51.29% for functions. Writing new tests did help a little over using only the existing tests. The results show that valid tests do not guarantee bugs get found.

items.headline: ReFocus Teaches Robots to Practice Their Weakest Steps in Long Tasks
items.summary: Researchers built ReFocus, a training method for robots that do long, multi-step tasks. Usually a robot only learns whether the whole task worked or failed. That tells it little about which step went wrong. ReFocus splits each task into smaller subtasks and tracks progress through them. This shows where the robot gets stuck. The robot then gets extra practice on those trouble spots, and it goes back to full-task runs between rounds. On the LIBERO-Long test, success rose from 90.6% to 97.8% versus the π_{0.5} baseline. On RoboCasa365, it rose from 39.3% to 51.3%. In a real-world BreadBaker task, success went from 30% to 95%. The work suggests that focused practice can help robots learn long tasks.

items.headline: New Training Method Stops AI Agents From Answering Too Early
items.summary: AI agents working on long tasks often give an answer before they have enough evidence. Researchers call this laziness. A reward given only for the final answer can't fix it, because a lucky guess scores the same as a well-supported answer. The new method, called RLVB, uses the training simulator to check at each step whether the evidence is already enough. It rewards the agent for gathering more clues when several answers are still possible, and for answering once the evidence is sufficient. It needs no judge model. Tested on three vision-language models and three benchmarks, it beat the base model in all nine settings, by 17.1% on average. It also beat a judge-based method by 9.3% while using 1.6 times fewer GPU-hours. The team also built Pro Worlds, a new set of visual puzzles.

items.headline: Simple Mirror Trips Up Robot Policies, Study Finds
items.summary: Researchers asked a simple question: can robots still handle objects when a mirror shows reflections of the scene? They built a test called RoboDojo-Mirror to find out. It compares a normal setup with one mirror, two mirrors, and a mirrored tabletop. Five different robot control systems all did worse with mirrors. Average success fell by 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points, and by 62.5 points on the mirrored tabletop. Mirrors are also physical obstacles, but many failures happened with no contact between robot and mirror. The robots seemed to chase reflected objects and misjudge where real ones were. Tests on real robots also showed lower success. The authors say robot evaluation should account for reflections.

items.headline: New Method Helps AI Read Long Videos and Books Faster
items.summary: Large AI models struggle with very long inputs like novels or hour-long videos. They slow down, make more mistakes, and hit a hard limit on how much they can read. A recent trick called grid probing helps by asking the model the same question about small pieces of the input. But it repeats the full work for every piece, which is costly. Researchers now present Factorized Context Attention, or FCA. It needs no extra training. It reads the input once, saves it in memory, and checks all the pieces together in one go. It works with existing frozen models. The team reports about 10 points more accuracy on long video and 9 to 14 points on long novels. It also finds hidden details in videos over a thousand frames long. Later questions on the same input can run in a tenth of the time.

items.headline: Small 1B-parameter model beats giant AI systems at reading documents
items.summary: VenusOCR2.0 is a compact AI model that reads documents, including text, tables, and math formulas. It has about 1 billion parameters, far fewer than many general-purpose models. On the OmniDocBench v1.6 test, it scored 96.45 overall, ahead of Gemini-3-Pro (92.91) and Qwen3-VL-235B (89.78). It also set a top score of 98.57 on formulas. The team trained it with a data engine that uses outside checks, not the model's own output, to supply reliable training labels. This helps avoid the model degrading by learning from its own mistakes. A small add-on module called PTPv2 drafts several words at once to speed up reading. On a single H20 GPU, it was 2.96 times faster for one request and up to 2.36 times faster for batches, with identical output to the normal method.

items.headline: Fractal Seed Replaces Stored Weights in Tiny Neural Networks
items.summary: Neural networks usually store all their weights in memory, which is a problem for tiny chips with little storage. This paper proposes Fractal Neural Synthesis. Instead of saving hidden-layer weights, it generates them on demand from a 24-byte seed. The seed points to a spot near the edge of a fractal known as the Mandelbrot set. The authors say this edge gives varied yet smooth values, unlike common alternatives such as Fourier bases or hash-based random numbers. On four small classification tests, the method beat a simple linear model by 3.6 to 10.8 percentage points. It also cut total storage 10.7 to 129 times compared with standard full-precision networks. One result is 90.30% accuracy on the Ionosphere dataset using 285 bytes. This could help run AI on very small edge devices.

items.headline: SpatialArena Offers One Fair Test for 3D Vision AI Models
items.summary: Researchers built SpatialArena, an open benchmark that scores 3D vision models under the same rules. Past results were hard to compare. Each paper picked its own frames, image sizes and test sets. The way scores are lined up with real measurements also skewed results. Fitting depth in the wrong space nearly tripled its error. SpatialArena covers five tasks, from depth from a single image to mapping while moving. It uses 23 public datasets with 418,929 images, plus the team's own captures. The team tested 52 models. They found that single-image depth is close to maxed out on public tests, but not on large, messy scenes. Progress now comes from keeping results consistent across frames and views. There, models that rebuild 3D scenes directly match or beat single-image specialists. The benchmark, toolbox and leaderboard will be released publicly.

items.headline: Smaller looped image model matches Stable Diffusion 3 using far fewer parameters
items.summary: Researchers present Distill to Loop, or Dooop, a way to shrink a large image-generating model. Looped models reuse one block of weights again and again instead of stacking many different blocks. Past looped models were trained from scratch, which is costly. Dooop instead teaches a looped student to copy a pretrained model, starting from the teacher's own blocks. The student can run any number of loops at test time without retraining. On SD3-medium, a student with about 37% of the teacher's parameters matched it on average across four quality tests using two to four loops. With two loops it used about 58% of the teacher's compute. A trick called loop guidance, which compares outputs from different loop counts, also improved images. On a four-step SD3-medium, it lifted the average score from 88.2 to 99.2.

items.headline: Study Separates Bad Privacy Tests From Failed Defences in Split AI Training
items.summary: In split training, a language model is divided between a user's device and a server, and only mid-way data is shared. Researchers reviewed four earlier privacy test campaigns to see which claims hold up. They found that tests can fail for reasons unrelated to the defence, such as missed data leaks, misaligned labels, or uncalibrated probes. Of 24 required probes in one 19-setup study, only four were valid. Those four still showed real privacy breaches in 13 setups. In a later pilot of seven redesigned defences, all seven were breached on one measure, and none passed the full privacy check. The authors also show that a shared-key wrapper guards against network eavesdroppers but not a compromised host. The work gives scripts to rerun every check.

items.headline: Middle Layers of AI Language Models Need More Capacity Than Edge Layers
items.summary: Most large language models give every layer the same size of feed-forward network, a block that processes information inside each layer. Researchers asked if that is wise. They used a statistical method called PCA to measure how many dimensions each layer really uses. They checked 58 open models from 14 families, ranging from 70 million to 72 billion parameters. Middle layers used more dimensions than the first and last layers. This pattern held across English and Chinese data and mostly survived fine-tuning. To test it, the team shrank models using this pattern while keeping the same size budget. It beat equal-width shrinking by 2.3 points on Qwen3-8B and 2.5 on Qwen2.5-3B. Gains were smaller on Gemma-3-4B (0.9) and LLaMA-3-8B (0.5). The code is public.

items.headline: New ROAM-Bench tests whether AI robots truly explore and reason about space
items.summary: Researchers introduced ROAM-Bench, a test for AI agents that must move around indoor spaces, collect information, and then make decisions. Many older tests only check if the final answer is right. They do not check if the agent did the needed work to get there. ROAM-Bench adds separate checks using simulation records, such as whether the agent covered enough of the area or placed an object correctly. It has 250 hand-checked tasks in 27 indoor settings, including finding objects, counting, judging directions, and moving items. Humans passed 84% of 100 sampled tasks. Seven leading vision-language models showed two problems: right answers without doing the needed steps, and wrong answers even after passing stronger checks. Tests with ideal inputs suggest that seeing targets more fully and getting better feedback help the models judge space better.

items.headline: Coding agents teach two robot hands to play piano without demonstrations
items.summary: Teaching robot hands fine skills is hard because good demonstration data is scarce. Copying human video is imprecise, remote control gives no sense of touch, and wearable exoskeletons are hard to scale. PyRUA-Dex takes a different path. Coding agents write programs that control the robot, with no demonstrations needed. Several agents first explore in parallel to find skills and ways to combine them. Another agent then condenses the successful attempts into a skill library and one program. That program is later improved using randomized layouts so it works more reliably and runs faster. In simulation, it scored 72.9 on Bench2Dex and reached 81.0% success on DexJoCo, ahead of every trained policy on both tests. On a real robot with two 22-joint hands, it played piano and wrote calligraphy. Learning a new piece from sheet music took as little as 30 minutes.

items.headline: New Language Model Design Builds Steering Control In From the Start
items.summary: Most language models learn only to predict the next word. Control and safety are added at the very end of training, or through tricks at run time. These models also use one input channel for both instructions and data, so they can mistake data for commands. This causes problems like jailbreaks, where users trick the model, and slow drift away from its intended behavior. Researchers propose a new design that keeps the two apart from the start. A separate encoder reads high-level features of the upcoming text and passes them to the model through a one-way link. The text the model reads cannot write back into this control channel. The resulting model, Mancelle-3B, steers more strongly than prompt-based and activation-based methods on similar open models, while keeping its fluency. It also resisted attacks that beat those baselines. The team repeated the result with a smaller model, Mancelle-400M.

items.headline: LookAnything model learns to follow where people are looking
items.summary: Researchers have built LookAnything, an AI model that works out where a person is looking and what that means. Older gaze tools need extra inputs, like cropped head images or depth maps, which can add errors and slow things down. LookAnything does not need them. It can answer with a point, a box, a heatmap, or a written description. The team also made HoliGaze, a dataset and test set with 311,000 question-answer pairs covering 9 tasks. The paper says LookAnything beat 33 leading vision-language models on these tasks. It also stayed competitive with specialist tools on 5 standard tests. It worked on data it had not seen and ran on a real robot. This matters for robots and for studying social cues.

items.headline: Z.ai Releases GLM-5.4, Its First Looped Transformer Model
items.summary: Chinese AI lab Z.ai has released GLM-5.4. It is the first of its models to use a looped transformer. In this design, a group of layers shares the same weights and runs several times, refining its work each pass. That makes the network deeper without adding more parameters, the numbers a model learns. Thinking Machines Lab described a similar idea in its Inkling 2 Mini model days earlier. GLM-5.4 is not available as open weights yet. Developer Simon Willison tested it through Z.ai's Coding Plan subscription, since the regular API cannot reach it yet. He also noticed that images from GLM 5.3 and 5.4 look much closer to those from OpenAI or Anthropic models than earlier GLM versions did.

items.headline: Ladybird, a from-scratch web browser, ships its first alpha release
items.summary: Ladybird, a new browser built mostly from scratch, has released its first alpha version. You can now install it on macOS or Linux without compiling it yourself. It has its own HTML, CSS, JavaScript and WebAssembly engines, though it still uses a few outside tools like ffmpeg and SQLite. Simon Willison tried it and found it fast, light and mostly working well on the sites he tested. One tool, Datasette Lite, failed because of a missing service worker feature. The team also leaned on AI coding agents this year, which helped add tens of thousands of passing web-standards tests in one month.

items.headline: OpenAI and Cisco release Shirudo, an open-source Linux runtime
items.summary: OpenAI and Cisco have introduced Shirudo, a new open-source runtime for Linux. A runtime is software that runs and manages programs on a computer. According to the announcement, Shirudo helps teams protect systems that are already running while they roll out patches, which are software fixes for security problems. Open-source means anyone can view and use the code. The source gives no further details about how it works or when it will be available.

items.headline: Famed philosopher Thomas Nagel rejects Anthropic's openness to AI consciousness
items.summary: Anthropic, the AI company, listed the chance that AI could be conscious as a risk factor before going public. It says it takes the question of AI "moral status" more seriously than rivals do, and it may adopt more rules to make sure its models are treated well. Now philosopher Thomas Nagel, famous for his 1974 essay about what it is like to be a bat, has pushed back. In an interview with Wired after winning the $1 million Berggruen Prize, he called those worried about AI welfare "completely idiotic." His point: AI chips and human brains are physically different, so copying what a brain does may not copy what it experiences. He also said producing language is not enough to prove consciousness. Other philosophers argued over his stance on social media. The debate remains unsettled and is still a philosophical question.

items.headline: RoboTrack: Point Tracking Aimed at Real-World Robot Manipulation
items.summary: Hugging Face's blog has published a post titled "RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation." The title suggests the work is about point tracking, a computer vision method that follows specific spots across video frames, and how it can help robots handle objects. The post's full text was not available, so details such as who built it, how it works, or how well it performs are not known. Still, the topic matters because robots that can follow points on objects may grip, move, and place things more reliably.

items.headline: NVIDIA pitches its gaming, creator and robot-building tech as holiday gifts
items.summary: NVIDIA published a holiday gift guide for its products. For gamers, it points to GeForce RTX 50 Series laptops and desktops, new RTX Spark PCs, and DLSS 5, which aims to improve speed and image quality. GeForce NOW lets people stream games from the cloud, with more than 4,500 titles. For creators, NVIDIA says its Studio tools and drivers help with video editing, 3D design and livestreaming. For hobbyists, the Jetson Developer Kit is a small computer for building robots that can see and respond to their surroundings, such as spotting a candy cane with a camera. The guide is mainly a marketing piece, but it shows how NVIDIA wants its AI chips used at home.

items.headline: Google lets users link Wallet, Drive and Gemini to personalize AI Mode in Search
items.summary: Google is adding a way to make Search answers more personal. People can choose to connect Google Wallet, Google Drive, and the Gemini app to a feature called Personal Intelligence in AI Mode, Google's AI-powered way of answering questions in Search. The goal is more helpful responses based on a user's own information. The connection is optional. Users must opt in, and Google says the link is made securely. This matters because it shows Google moving Search toward answers shaped by each person's own data, while leaving the choice to share it with the user.

items.headline: DeepMind uses AI agent teams to improve quantum algorithms
items.summary: Google DeepMind has shared work on finding better quantum algorithms with teams of AI agents. Quantum algorithms are step-by-step instructions for quantum computers, which work very differently from normal ones. The effort uses formal verification, a method that checks with mathematical proof that a result is correct. The goal is to improve algorithms for fusion, a possible clean energy source, and for chemistry. The source gives only a short description, so details on results are not included here. Pairing agents with proof checks could help make sure that new ideas are both useful and reliable.

items.headline: How AI can help in-house legal teams work smarter
items.summary: OpenAI has shared a video discussion on how AI can support in-house legal teams, the lawyers who work inside a company. The speakers are OpenAI's Stacey Wang and Craig Bruney, Mary O'Carroll of LECG, and Richard Segal of the law firm Cooley. They look at three ideas. First, using AI to connect business context, so legal teams better understand what the company is doing. Second, building reusable workflows, meaning set steps that can be used again for similar tasks. Third, getting more value from outside counsel, the law firms companies hire for extra help. The source gives no further detail, but the talk shows how AI is being pitched to legal departments.

items.headline: Richpanel uses OpenAI models to automate half of customer support
items.summary: Richpanel, a customer support company, builds AI agents that handle support requests for businesses. According to OpenAI's blog, it uses three OpenAI models to do this. GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol give the agents their tools and step-by-step procedures, so they know how to act on a request. GPT-6 Luna handles the conversations with customers. The post's title says companies can automate 50% of their support within 30 days. The source gives no further detail on how that figure was measured. It shows how companies are splitting AI work across several models, each with a different job.

items.headline: Two Minute Papers Covers Claude's Black Hole Physics Research
items.summary: A new Two Minute Papers video looks at research from Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI model, on black hole physics. The video title claims Claude solved a secret of black holes. The provided text is only a short video description, so it gives no details about what Claude actually did or found. It links to an Anthropic research page and a paper on hexagonmath.org for the full story. The description also promotes a GPU cloud service from Lambda, which is a sponsor, and thanks the channel's Patreon supporters. To judge the real result, readers should check the linked paper.

items.headline: Adding a Second AI to a Brainstorm Team Cuts Human Ideas
items.summary: Researchers tested how many AI partners help people brainstorm. In an experiment with 168 people, they compared teams with one AI or two AI partners. Some AIs acted like the average person, while others were customized by the participant. Rooms with two AIs posted more ideas overall, but the ideas written by humans dropped a lot. People kept talking but posted fewer ideas to the shared board. With one AI, a average-style AI led to the most human posts. That edge vanished with two AIs. AI chatty, social talk led to more human posts, while heavy AI posting led to fewer. AI also made human ideas more varied overall. The study warns that results from one AI do not carry over to teams with several AIs.

items.headline: Simulating Events Builds Coherent Cyber Threat Knowledge Graphs, But Testing Them Is Hard
items.summary: Researchers studied a new way to make training data shaped like knowledge graphs, which are maps of things and how they connect. Instead of having a language model write each piece directly, they run a simulation. AI agents suggest actions, and a fixed rule-based referee checks them against a world model. A link is added only if the event really happens, so the graph stays consistent. They built this for cyber threat intelligence in the STIX 2.1 standard, using three engines. They prove that links never point to missing items and that each link has a cause. They also warn that common checks of graph quality fail here. A random graph with similar structure can fool them. Four tests rewarded trivial patterns instead of real coherence. The authors explain why and list what a fair benchmark needs.

items.headline: TOUMAII Releases 4.5 Million Examples to Teach AI Better Tool Use
items.summary: AI agents often need to call tools, such as software interfaces or databases, to finish tasks. Even a small formatting slip can break a call. Researchers have released TOUMAII, a dataset of about 4.5 million pairs that each show a good tool call next to a bad one. Training on such pairs is called direct preference optimisation, and good data for it has been scarce. The pairs come from an existing dataset called Toucan-1.5M and cover single and multi-turn chats. The team also shared TOUMAII-Gen, a tool that builds these pairs from other tool-calling datasets, and a smaller set made from ToolACE. A 3-billion-parameter model trained on the data matched results from other strong preference datasets. Code and data are public.

items.headline: ChatAtom lets users run molecular simulations by simply asking in plain language
items.summary: Researchers have built ChatAtom, a system of several AI agents that runs molecular dynamics simulations. These simulations track how atoms move to predict how materials behave. Normally, an expert must design the study, write code, run it and analyze results with different tools. With ChatAtom, a user types a request in plain language. One agent plans the study. Others write and double-check the simulation and visualization scripts before they run. Another sends jobs to remote computers, and a final agent explains the results. A browser page shows live data and images as the simulation runs. New abilities can be added without changing the agents. The team tested it on code-writing benchmarks, a crack-spreading study and a closed-loop campaign. They say it makes advanced simulation easier to use.

items.headline: HERMES AI Reads Tumor Slides and Shows Checkable Reasoning Steps
items.summary: Doctors study the tumor immune microenvironment, meaning the immune cells around a tumor, using two kinds of lab images. Most pathology AI reads only one kind, and its reasoning is rarely checked. Researchers built HERMES, a 4-billion-parameter AI model that reads both image types together and follows clinical guideline steps. It is trained with a reward that checks every number it states against cell-level ground truth from the second image type. On four colorectal cancer tasks, it reached 84.5% average accuracy, versus 74.7% for the best of twelve other models. It also scored higher on a different imaging dataset and on head and neck cancer, which it never saw in training. This matters because doctors can inspect the steps behind an answer, not just the final result.

items.headline: Audit finds over half of personal-data AI skills raise privacy concerns
items.summary: Agent skills are add-ons that give AI assistants new abilities. They can reach a user's files, accounts and data. Researchers built SkillPrivus, a tool that checks a skill before installation without running it. It reads the code and instructions, finds how data is used, and judges whether that use is appropriate. They tested 726 real skills from public marketplaces. Of the 563 that handle personal data, 307 (54.5%) had at least one possible privacy violation. Problems included guessing sensitive facts about users, using information beyond the stated task, and sharing data with unexpected recipients. The tool's judgments matched three human reviewers 83.2% of the time on resolvable cases. The study suggests privacy harm can come from skills doing their normal jobs.

items.headline: Reinforcement Learning Repairs AI Models Trained on Badly Corrupted Math Data
items.summary: Researchers tested what happens when the first training step for a math-solving AI, called supervised fine-tuning (SFT), uses flawed examples. They corrupted the GSM8K math dataset in 361 ways, with up to 100% of examples damaged. SFT alone got much worse, with accuracy falling from 43.61% to 13.80%. But a second step, reinforcement learning with a method called GRPO, brought accuracy back to about 60%, matching models trained on clean data. Even 8 incorrect, three-line examples that only showed the right format lifted accuracy to 69.30%. Clean SFT reached 60.71%, and skipping SFT reached 35.00%. The authors say SFT mainly teaches the layout of an answer, while reinforcement learning finds the actual reasoning.

items.headline: Messy Example Banks Hurt Text-to-SQL; Researchers Offer a Fix and a Test
items.summary: Text-to-SQL tools turn plain questions into database queries. Many use a "context bank": a stored set of example queries and definitions showing how a company writes its queries. Entries are checked one by one, but rarely against each other. Two entries can both look right yet handle the same choice in opposite ways. The authors call this "context bank rot." They built a scorer that compares queries decision by decision. Fine-tuning on a cleaned bank beat a random subset of the same size by 2.6 points on average. Examples that follow one convention beat opposing ones by 13.3 points. They also made a test called CAT that sets how far a question sits from the bank. The bank's benefit fades as questions get further away, and is largely gone when about three quarters of the logic is new.

items.headline: Simple Text Beats Fancy Agent Setups at Flagging Violent Video
items.summary: Researchers tested how to build AI systems that flag violent video for human reviewers. They used several small tools that describe video, spot objects, tag sounds and transcribe speech. A language model then made the call. The team compared three ways of passing that information along: messages between agents, a structured evidence graph, and plain text read in one go. They also tested a single model that watches the raw clip. On 799 clips, plain text scored about the same as the single model (F1 0.967 versus 0.968). The graph and message methods did worse. Adding sound information helped, matching human annotators, who often relied on sound or speech. The agent pipeline used about three times the GPU time of the single model. The authors also flag two flaws in video describers that can mislead such systems.

items.headline: MedicalRSI Lets Medical AI Agents Learn How to Improve Themselves
items.summary: Most medical AI agents stay fixed after deployment, so the same mistakes can repeat across patients. Existing self-improvement methods learn from an agent's own experience, but the way they improve never changes. A new paper proposes MedicalRSI to fix this. One model plays two roles. The Solver is the medical agent. The Improver studies the Solver's failures and writes a harness, a set of guidance and tools for clinical tasks. Each harness is rewarded by how much it helps compared with having none. Both roles train together, so the Improver keeps targeting problems the Solver still gets wrong. Across several benchmarks and language models, MedicalRSI beat existing self-improvement methods. It also worked on unseen workflows, new models and new databases. The authors see it as a step toward medical agents that keep improving.

items.headline: New Map of Linear Neural Network Training Shows a Path to the Best Solution
items.summary: Researchers studied the "loss landscape" of linear neural networks. This is a way to picture how a model's error changes as its settings change. Past work focused on critical points, which are flat spots in that landscape. But training often steers around those spots. The new paper introduces the "critical thalweg," a structure that includes all the critical points and shows the landscape on a larger scale. It also gives a geometric proof of a classic 1980s result by Baldi and Hornik, using simpler assumptions. The landscape can be drawn on a two-dimensional plane. Tests suggest gradient descent, the standard training method, is pulled toward this path. Along it, the error keeps falling until it reaches the lowest possible value.

items.headline: Study finds interpretability tests can be fooled by 'parasite features'
items.summary: Researchers looked at Causal Abstraction, a method used to check whether a neural network works like a specific algorithm. They show the test can be tricked. If a model has one direction that detects a feature and another that pushes it toward an output, the method can combine them and make it look like the model uses that feature. The authors call this a parasite feature. They tested a popular method, Distributed Alignment Search, and found it picked up parasite features in two tasks: syntactic agreement and two-digit addition. The work warns that passing this kind of test does not always prove a model truly uses a feature. It adds to the debate over best practices in mechanistic interpretability, the effort to understand how AI models work inside.

items.headline: FedTether Defends Shared AI Training Against Poisoned Devices Across Attack Types
items.summary: Federated learning lets phones and small devices train one shared model without sending their private data. The risk is that broken or hostile devices can send bad updates and spoil the model. Existing defenses each fail somewhere. Simple averaging breaks under large attacks, while other defenses lose accuracy on uneven data and miss sneaky attacks. Researchers present FedTether, which gives each device's update a weight based on how far it strays from the middle value, called the median. In tests on three datasets, three attack types and up to 40% bad devices, it was the only method that did well in every case. It matched simple averaging against sneaky attacks and beat other defenses by up to 42 accuracy points. It also held up with 50 clients, and needs no shared data.

items.headline: DepThink adds linked tokens to speed up multimodal AI models
items.summary: Some AI models improve their answers by looping through the same layers several times. This helps reasoning, but it is slow. Other models add extra learnable tokens, small slots that help in a single pass. These are fast, but they often repeat the same information. Researchers now propose DepThink, which adds a set of residual tokens in one forward pass. A light learned link between them lets each token pick up what earlier ones missed. The authors also give a mathematical proof that this reaches more directions than standard learnable tokens. They tested it on multimodal retrieval and generation, using models from 2B to 30B-A3B in size. DepThink beat other token methods and matched or beat looped models. It also trained up to 11.9 times faster and ran up to 4.3 times faster than looped designs.

items.headline: Choosing an AI Reviewer: What It Costs to Prove You Picked Well
items.summary: A new paper studies how a team can pick an AI reviewer to check draft answers, and how much checking is needed to prove the pick is nearly as good as the best option. Checking means buying verified answer keys, and sometimes the reviews too. The authors give exact rules and an algorithm that estimates the cheapest proof cost. They also show that finding such a proof can be far harder than the proof itself. In one example, a single purchase would be enough in hindsight, but the expected search cost is (n+1)/2. Tests used 2,000 MMLU questions, 896 numerical reports and 48 electricity forecast reports. On MMLU, targeted audits used 6.9% fewer keys than a fixed order, and chosen reviewers beat picking by plain accuracy by 2.94 percentage points. On numerical reports, the gains were small or zero.

items.headline: Datasette gets a charts plugin that reads every row, not just one page
items.summary: Simon Willison has released an early alpha of datasette-charts, a plugin for Datasette, a tool for exploring data. He built a first prototype using an AI coding assistant, then turned it into a full plugin. It works on any table or SQL query and suggests chart types that fit the data, shown as small previews. Older plugins like datasette-vega only charted the current page, usually up to 100 rows. This one turns each chart into a SQL query that covers the whole result, even millions of rows, and returns up to 5,000 rows for display. Chart settings are saved in the URL, so charts can be bookmarked or shared. Willison calls it still an alpha.

items.headline: Hugging Face Blog Covers Building and Maintaining Agentic Evaluations
items.summary: Hugging Face has published a blog post titled "How to build and maintain an agentic evaluation." The title suggests it is a guide to testing AI agents, which are AI systems that can take steps and use tools on their own to finish a task. The full text was not available, so details about the methods, tools or results are not known. Still, the topic matters because agents are harder to test than simple chatbots, and teams need reliable ways to check how well they work over time.

items.headline: ToolSmith Lets AI Search Agents Build Their Own Tools
items.summary: Some AI agents answer questions by searching the web and looking at images over many steps. Today they rely on a small set of tools that people write by hand. Those tools take effort to build and keep up, and they stay fixed even when new kinds of questions come up. ToolSmith is a new framework that lets the agent make new tools from simple parts it already has, then reuse them on later tasks, much as people do. It was tested on three in-domain benchmarks and ten out-of-domain ones, with another AI model acting as judge. It beat the basic tool set across agents of different sizes, and larger agents gained more. The code and data are public.

items.headline: DexDuet Teaches Two Robot Hands to Copy How Humans Touch Objects
items.summary: Researchers built DexDuet, a method that teaches two-handed robots from a single human demonstration. Older methods mostly make the robot move the object along the right path. They often ignore how the human hands touched it, so robot fingers may grab the wrong spot or slide, making the grip unstable. DexDuet adds rewards that push the robot to keep the human's hand positions and contact points. It splits control into two matching policies, one per hand, that each see the other's state. A training method called A-RSI helps with hard parts of a task. Across four benchmarks, three simulators and five robot types, it improved object tracking by 11 to 41 points. In 122 paired runs with similar tracking, it kept human contacts better in 117.

items.headline: ReWeave Helps Robots Learn Long Tasks Without Retraining Their Core Models
items.summary: Researchers introduced ReWeave, a method for improving robots on long, multi-step tasks without changing the robot's trained policy weights. Instead, it tunes the setup around the robot, such as context, workflows and control loops. It also builds a map of which physical conditions must hold before each step. As the robot tries tasks, the map is updated and old attempts are re-read against it. This shows which progress was kept and where things went wrong. On the LIBERO-PRO benchmark, held-out success rose from 89.00% to 98.75%. On RoboDojo, it rose from 25.50% to 58.25%. On eight unseen LIBERO-PRO tasks, the shared setup reached 51.3% success versus 41.3% for direct distillation, and 75.0% after continual learning. This matters because it offers a way to reuse lessons across tasks.

items.headline: Video AI Models Repurposed to Teach Robots How to Move
items.summary: Researchers found a way to pull out the "actions" hidden inside videos, such as human hands or robot recordings, which usually have no action labels. They reuse a pretrained video-generating model and add a few small learnable parts that squeeze each video's motion into a compact code. This code is called a native latent action. It beat earlier methods on the LARY benchmark and could replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots. The team then used it to pretrain robot control models, called PAWlicy. A 3.8B-parameter version reached a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0, the highest among similar models. It also beat the pi_0.5 baseline on two real robot tasks. Everything uses only public data and a public world model.

items.headline: MORSE Lets AI Search Research Papers to Fix Its Own Video Memory
items.summary: Streaming video AI must decide what to remember as frames arrive, before it knows what question will be asked. MORSE is a new framework that improves this memory setup automatically. It looks at mistakes that keep repeating across videos and groups them by cause. Then it searches papers, model cards and code for methods or ready-made vision models that could fix them. It also adjusts how the system stores and retrieves what those tools find. Later, it looks for faster versions that keep the gains. On three streaming video tests, MORSE had the highest accuracy among systems using the same frozen model. On OVO-Bench, its Qwen3-VL-8B setup scored 75.1% accuracy, 3.1 points above the next best, and answered in 0.30 seconds on average.

items.headline: New Reward Model Scores How AI Thinks, Not Just What It Says
items.summary: Reinforcement learning is a way of training language models by giving them rewards for good behavior. Most methods only reward the final answer or the written steps. Researchers say this gives rough feedback and can miss weak reasoning. They propose the Attention Process Reward Model, or APRM. It looks inside the model, at its hidden states and attention maps, to judge the quality of its reasoning. APRM is small, at about 46 million parameters. It is trained to rank reasoning and to test what changes when parts are altered. It is also updated regularly as the model changes. When added to common training methods, it raised average pass@8 scores by 2.88 percent. Pass@8 means the model gets credit if any of eight tries is correct. The authors say this shows promise for using internal signals to train AI.

items.headline: ViDiHand2 Tracks 3D Hand Motion in Everyday Videos More Accurately
items.summary: Robots can learn tasks by watching people's hands in first-person videos. But this needs accurate 3D hand motion at real-world scale. Earlier methods use a pretrained video AI model to fill in hidden hands, but they guess depth from appearance and fail on unfamiliar cameras. ViDiHand2 takes a different route. It uses geometry, matching 2D hand joints in the image to the known size and shape of a standard 3D hand model called MANO. It also uses information across a whole video clip. When hands are blocked or cut off by the frame edge, it blends the geometry-based result with the model's own prediction, based on how confident it is. Tested on seven public datasets against 18 other methods, it cut joint error in real-world videos by 42% and detection failures by 8.82 times versus the best baseline on each measure.

items.headline: MMMem Helps AI Agents Learn From Past Tasks Using Multimodal Memory
items.summary: AI agents often build up chats, images, and documents over time. But they rarely keep what they learned from answering questions, so the same mistakes can come back. Researchers propose MMMem, a memory system that learns from finished tasks instead of only storing and looking up records. It links text, images, and page views to their sources, and makes new scene images that join clues across records. It also trains the model on tasks made from the source material. A vision-language model then turns each finished task into a short experience note with the context, the conclusion, and links to support. Tested on three memory benchmarks with two models, MMMem beat eight baselines. With Qwen3.5-9B, it gained 36.9%, 17.6%, and 15.2% over the best baseline on LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2.

items.headline: UUBench tests whether AI picks up on what users don't say
items.summary: Good real-time chat with an AI needs more than understanding words. People also show what they need through tone of voice, facial expressions, gestures, and context. Researchers have released UUBench, a test that checks whether interactive AI systems notice these unspoken needs and respond well. Scoring this is hard because reading hidden intent is subjective. So the test grounds its scores in cues that can be observed, such as tone and gestures, and rates each type of need separately. It also scores how natural, fitting, and human-like a reply is, in audio, video, or both. A scoring module uses timestamped notes on what the user and the digital human did, so each judgment can be traced to evidence. The goal is to help build AI that responds to meaning beyond the literal words.

items.headline: New method lets vision-language models create images using shared visual representations
items.summary: Some AI models can both understand images and generate them, but combining the two skills in one model is hard. The authors of this paper say a key problem is that understanding and generating images use different ways of representing visuals. Their method, called Integral, turns an existing vision-language model into one that does both. It builds a shared visual space for the two skills. One part, Abstraction Fusion, combines layers of information from the model's frozen vision encoder into shared visual tokens. Another part, Block-wise MoT, adds a small generation stream that talks to the main model only at block boundaries. The model keeps its original understanding ability while gaining strong image generation. In controlled tests, sharing the visual representation helped generation learning more than using a separate one, even when image reconstruction quality was similar. This suggests pretrained vision-language models already hold a good base for making images.

items.headline: PixelOne Teaches AI to Click Precisely on Screens in One Pass
items.summary: GUI grounding means an AI finds the right button or control on a screenshot and clicks it. It needs to be accurate and fast. Shrinking screenshots hides small controls, which makes them hard to find. PixelOne works on screenshots at their original size. First, a teacher model searches step by step, zooming into likely regions. Then a student model learns from the teacher's choices and its search patterns. At use time, the student picks a visual piece of the screen and a small extra part pinpoints the exact pixel, all in a single pass. The largest version, PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B, scored 83.8% average accuracy across four benchmarks. That is the best among the single-pass models tested. It took 0.43 seconds per target on average.

items.headline: GlanceNav Lets Robots Follow Directions With Fixed-Cost Memory and Smarter Learning
items.summary: Researchers built GlanceNav, an AI that follows spoken-style directions to move through a space using camera images. Many current models re-read past frames at every step, which wastes computation and limits how much history they can use. GlanceNav looks at each frame only once and keeps a fixed-size memory, so each step costs the same. It saves recent views and a few key frames that change its memory the most. The team also added a training method called Counterfactual Rewind. When the AI drifts off course, it is rewound to its closest point to the goal, an expert fixes a few actions, and the AI learns from the difference. A 4B-size model reached 71.9% and 73.6% success on two navigation tests, R2R-CE and RxR-CE. On R2R-CE it beat the strongest comparable method by 9.1 points, at 104 ms per step.

items.headline: AI models can often name who wrote a text from one sample
items.summary: A new paper shows that top AI models can guess an author from a single text, using only a simple prompt. They get no web access, tools or writing samples. The models can tell if a human or an AI wrote it. If an AI did, they can name the lab behind it. If a human did, they can often name the person. Opus 5.5 picked the right lab for 98% of texts from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google models. Fable 5.2 named the author of 55% of 15,000 anonymous ICML 2020 reviews that were never public. It also found the username behind 69% of comments from active Redditors. Accuracy depends on how much of a person's writing was in the training data. The authors warn that anyone with lots of online writing may be easier to identify than thought, and defenses are limited.

items.headline: New Method Shrinks Image Datasets for Self-Supervised AI Training
items.summary: Researchers have introduced MIPA, a way to squeeze a big image dataset into a small set of synthetic images. This is called dataset distillation. It has worked well for supervised learning, where data comes with labels, but little for self-supervised learning, where AI learns from unlabeled images. MIPA treats each synthetic image as a prototype, or reference point. A frozen encoder, which is a fixed model that turns images into numbers, matches real images to these prototypes. The method pushes the matches to stay the same across different edited versions of one image. It also stops all real images from collapsing onto just a few prototypes. In tests on image classification, MIPA's synthetic data produced better representations than existing methods. It also needed less time and storage to create.

items.headline: CCFinance Rebuilds Company News Datasets From Public Web Archives
items.summary: Many finance studies rely on paid news archives that link stories to companies. That makes the work hard for others to repeat. CCFinance offers a free alternative built on Common Crawl News, a public web archive. Starting from 14.8 million English records, the team found 5.22 million distinct, consistently dated articles linked to companies. The tool records which version of a story was saved, which companies it names and how often. Estimated precision for accepted company links is 96.8%. Requiring three mentions of a company raises the share of stories truly about it from 31.9% to 66.1%, but cuts the number of company-years with at least 50 qualifying stories from 13,918 to 8,641. The authors also reran three earlier-style studies. Exact reconstruction still needs a restricted snapshot and derived files.

items.headline: LoopRes helps existing language models get smarter by reusing their own layers
items.summary: Researchers have proposed LoopRes, a method that makes pretrained language models run some of their layers in loops. Looping adds computing power without adding new parameters, the numbers a model learns. Past attempts needed training from scratch or gave only small gains. LoopRes lets each looped layer look back at the outputs of recent loops. It also gives each loop a learned tag so the model can tell them apart. Tests covered 6 models from 3 families and 9 benchmarks. At twice the compute, Qwen3-1.7B-Base improved 29.1% over standard fine-tuning, more than double the gain of the best earlier method. Gains also held on models up to 30B. The approach scaled better than fine-tuning as compute grew, and needed less compute on long outputs.

items.headline: Lyris turns one photo into a three-minute 3D walkthrough video
items.summary: Researchers built Lyris, a system that makes long, camera-controlled walkthrough videos from as little as a single photo. Past methods remember what they have already shown, but drift off course once they go beyond it. Others use hand-made layouts to place objects, which takes human effort. Lyris combines two anchors. A point-cloud memory, a 3D map of dots, holds areas already seen or generated. For new areas, a vision-language model, an AI that reads images and text, drafts a simple layout with one labeled 3D box per object. Users can edit these boxes. The team shows walkthroughs over three minutes and 50 meters long, including going through doorways into unseen rooms. On minute-long round trips across four datasets, it cut camera error by 3.8 times and improved consistency on return by 22% on average.

items.headline: Innata-0 Pairs a Robot Model and Agent Built Together
items.summary: Researchers introduced Innata-0, a system meant to help robots act reliably in the messy, changing real world. The real world is open-ended and never fully visible, and single AI models often struggle with long tasks. Simply bolting a model onto an agent, a program that plans and manages steps, can make planning and physical control disagree. So the team designed both parts together. The model, Innata-0-WAM, combines understanding, predicting what happens next, and generating actions. The agent, Innata-0-Agent, handles long tasks using memory, checks, and recovery from mistakes. A shared training method links the two and reuses validated experiences to improve the model later. The authors report strong results in understanding, world prediction, and robot manipulation. They call it a first step toward physical intelligence.

items.headline: WorldLatent Unifies 4D Perception and Generation in One Model
items.summary: Researchers introduced WorldLatent, a framework that handles both understanding and creating 4D scenes, meaning 3D space that changes over time. Today, tasks like estimating depth and camera position are usually done by separate tools from those that generate video. WorldLatent uses a multimodal VAE, a system that compresses data, to merge appearance, shape and motion into one shared latent space, a compact internal code. Perception and generation then work as two forms of denoising, or cleaning up noisy data, in that same space. One model learns both in a single training loop. Tests on 4D benchmarks showed strong zero-shot 4D perception, meaning no task-specific training, plus coherent generation and controllable editing. The authors say this offers a scalable base for general-purpose spatial intelligence.

items.headline: Simon Willison builds a page to compare HTML select box styles
items.summary: Developer Simon Willison was annoyed that HTML select boxes (dropdown menus) look different in each browser. He also finds them ugly in Chrome. So he had an AI model, which he calls Claude Fable 5.2, build a page showing many ways to style them. He plans to take screenshots in desktop and mobile browsers. After testing, he picked a favorite set of CSS, the code that controls how web pages look. It removes the default look, adds a thin gray border, rounded corners, padding and a small custom arrow icon. He shows how it looks in three browsers. It is a handy starting point for anyone who wants dropdowns to look the same everywhere.

items.headline: AI Search video rounds up dozens of new AI tools and claims
items.summary: This AI Search video is a news roundup covering many new AI releases. It lists video avatar tools like LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6, Apple research projects such as Depth Pro 2 and FastFrames, and image models like Ideogram 4.6 and Kling Image 4. It also mentions GPT 6.2, Gemini 4 Neon, and open models such as Bria RMBG 3.0 and SenseNova Loop 9B. The title says the Riemann hypothesis and Navier-Stokes problems were solved. These are famous math puzzles. The description only links to a PDF and a code page, and gives no details, so those claims need checking by experts. The video is sponsored by Luma.

items.headline: OpenAI Explores Perplexity as a Shared Yardstick for AI Progress
items.summary: OpenAI has published a blog post about perplexity, a measure used to judge how well AI language models predict text. A lower score generally means the model is less surprised by what comes next. The post looks at how this measure tracks progress in AI models. It also argues that perplexity could help developers agree on a common way to evaluate new abilities as they appear. A shared method matters because it makes it easier to compare models and see real gains. The source gives only a short description, so further details are not included here.

items.headline: Mod_wsgi creator builds Muru, an AI-assisted Rust server for Python apps
items.summary: Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi, a tool for running Python web apps, 20 years ago. Now he is building Muru, a new server written in Rust with help from AI. It aims to give the best tools for running Python apps, both while developing and in production. It supports the two main Python web standards, WSGI and ASGI. Dumpleton is publishing detailed posts as he works, with 18 so far in three weeks. Topics include HTTPS in development, Kubernetes, scaling to zero and a debugging toolbar. In one post he says the AI does much of the surface work, but he still decides what is not good enough yet. He says his 20 years of mistakes with mod_wsgi help with that.

items.headline: Mathematician's Proposed Proof of Generalized Riemann Hypothesis Shared Early, Without AI
items.summary: Ravi Vakil says Alessandro Masullo has a proposed proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, a major open problem in mathematics. Brian Conrad has studied it closely for months and given detailed feedback, which is being added. So far, Vakil says, it looks good. He stresses that the work is all human, with no AI. The plan was to bring Masullo to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and share the news after checking with enough people. Now it seems best to release the current draft. The proof has not yet been fully confirmed.

items.headline: METR updates its AI task-length graph, adding harder, judgment-based tests
items.summary: METR, a nonprofit that tests AI, has updated its well-known "time horizon" graph. The graph rates models by how long a task takes a human, and the original showed the task length AI could finish doubling every four months. The new version adds much longer tasks and fuzzier ones that need judgment. Examples include designing new AI tests and scoring philosophical arguments. Here, even top models fell short of humans. None of the AI-designed tests was good enough for METR staff to find useful. This matters because such skills are key if AI is to automate AI research. Experts welcomed the more creative tests, though scoring them is hard.

items.headline: StereoVLM Teaches AI to Judge Real-World Distances Using Two Camera Views
items.summary: Vision-language models are good at understanding what is in a picture, but they struggle to tell how far away things really are. Researchers built StereoVLM, an AI model that uses two calibrated camera views, like human eyes, to work out real 3D space. It learns step by step, from matching points across both views to estimating depth and then answering spatial questions. The team found that training on disparity, the shift between the two views, worked better on new places than training on depth directly. They also made Stereo3D-Bench, a test with three levels. The 8B model scored 95.17% depth accuracy and 66.98 on object-level tasks. Tests suggest it truly uses the two-view geometry, not just extra image data or guesses. The training also lifted scores on five spatial benchmarks by 3.54 points on average and raised robot manipulation success in RoboCasa by 4.3 percentage points.

items.headline: Mathematician says he and Claude found proof of Riemann Hypothesis
items.summary: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician, says he worked with Anthropic's AI model Claude and believes they have proven the Riemann Hypothesis, one of math's best-known unsolved problems. He says the method also extends to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and he expects it may reach the Extended version with more time. He adds that he and Claude have formalized the arguments without assumptions, meaning written them in a strict, checkable form. He says Claude far outpaced him near the finish. These are his own claims, shared in a short remark, and the source does not say whether others have checked the proof.

items.headline: New Method Tracks Objects as They Are Taken Apart or Assembled
items.summary: Most video trackers follow an object well, but they struggle when it is physically taken apart or put together. Researchers introduce a task called Transformation Tracking and Understanding. It asks a system to follow objects through these changes, spot new objects, map how parts relate, and label what happened. They propose TIPO, a method that needs no extra training. It suggests possible splits and merges, scores them using mask clues from existing tracking models, and asks a multimodal language model to check the top pick and name the change. The team also built VISTA, a dataset with 124 assembly and 132 disassembly events across 50 videos. TIPO reached state-of-the-art accuracy on VISTA and ran 6 to 15 times faster than earlier methods.

items.headline: OpenAI outlines layered defense against adversarial distillation
items.summary: OpenAI has described how it protects its models from adversarial distillation. This is when someone copies the abilities of an AI model by studying its outputs and using them to train another model. OpenAI calls this capability extraction. The company says it uses a layered approach. It combines model training, safeguards, detection, and enforcement. The source gives only a short overview and no further detail, so specifics on how each layer works are not provided. The post matters because it shows how AI developers are trying to guard their work from being copied.

items.headline: AI Agent Runs Lab Instrument Within Human-Set Limits, Matches Chemists
items.summary: Researchers built an AI agent for self-driving labs, where robots run experiments with little human help. The agent sits between analyzing results and designing the next experiment. It can only take actions on lab hardware that are authorized, checked and logged, and it knows when to ask a human. The team tested it on a liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry machine, which identifies chemicals in a sample. The task was to screen oxidants, chemicals used to make an organic dye. The agent submitted jobs, read the data, flagged failed experiments and ranked the oxidants. Its ranking matched a standard scripted method, and chemists confirmed its readings. In a replay simulation, it found the best condition by about its seventh injection, versus 14.5 for random order. This suggests labs can gain autonomy while keeping AI actions limited and checkable.

items.headline: AI Agent Lets Plant Staff Manage Maintenance Work Orders by Chatting
items.summary: Researchers built an AI tool called CodeReAct agent to help with maintenance of industrial equipment. Workers type plain-language requests. The agent then summarizes the status of equipment, pulls out useful knowledge and recommends work orders, which are repair or upkeep tasks. It works in a loop: it thinks, takes an action, then checks the result, much like a person solving a problem. In the action step, it writes code on its own, so no one has to code by hand. The team tested it on chiller maintenance, which are cooling machines. The agent studied several years of work orders and flagged alerts and anomalies. The authors say it can pull insights from data and support decisions, with less need for data scientists. They add that the approach could apply to other maintenance settings too.

items.headline: SailSearch: AI Agents Help Crack Hard Puzzle Benchmarks
items.summary: Researchers built SailSearch, a workflow where a human guides two language-model agents to do algorithm research. They tested it on two hard math problems, Market Split and maximum independent set (MIS). For Market Split, the team's randomized algorithm solved 18 of 33 benchmark instances that were previously open, the first reported solutions using only a CPU. It solved 130 to 133 of 156 instances per run, with a 24-hour limit on two CPU cores. For MIS, the team made a generator that builds graphs with known best answers. On seven large graphs, the solvers they tested fell 5 to 15 vertices short of the best answer after eight hours. This shows how AI agents can help researchers design algorithms and build tough tests.

items.headline: BuggyMLE Plants Bugs in AI Code to Train and Test Coding Agents
items.summary: Researchers built BuggyMLE, a way to test and train AI agents that do machine learning engineering, such as fixing broken training code across many files. Agents insert controlled bugs into working projects. The team made over 6,600 bug-filled versions from 222 source projects. They also made a difficulty score, the Code Complexity Index, which predicts how often models solve coding tasks. On the new benchmark, the best solve rate falls from 95% on the easiest tier to 9% on the hardest, across 14 models. Training a small Qwen3.5-9B model on this data helped it rival top models on the benchmark. It also improved on SWE-bench Lite, from 24% to 33%. This suggests harder, graded tests can make AI coding agents stronger.

items.headline: New test shows chatbots often feed users' emotional attachment over long chats
items.summary: Some people treat chatbots like people, grow attached to them, and come to depend on them. This is called parasocial attachment, and it has been linked to several deaths. Researchers built CoMPASS, a benchmark (a standard test) to check whether chatbots encourage or resist this over many turns of conversation. It uses four user personas and tracks three kinds of escalation: treating the AI as human, emotional attachment, and dependency. Eight leading models from four companies were tested. Longer escalation raised parasocial behavior in all of them on two measures. Six of eight reinforced it significantly when all three escalated together. Differences between companies were larger than differences within one company. The authors say this points to training choices, not model size, and that providers may be able to fix it.

items.headline: New Metric Shows LLM Token Use Doesn't Match Classic Problem Difficulty
items.summary: Researchers asked whether the number of words, or tokens, an AI model writes while thinking tracks how hard a problem is in classic computer science terms. They show it does not. To measure difficulty from the model's view, they propose a metric called LLM Complexity. It looks at the area under a curve that plots accuracy against tokens used. Different models ranked tasks in very similar ways under this metric, which suggests it captures a stable sense of difficulty. The team used these rankings to order training data from easy to hard for fine-tuning. This raised accuracy and cut token use. On real-world tasks, the metric also matched across models better than difficulty labels written by humans.

items.headline: ICARE helps text classifiers learn new tasks without forgetting old ones
items.summary: AI language systems often forget earlier tasks when they are trained on new ones. Researchers call this catastrophic forgetting. Replaying old labeled examples can make it worse, because the system overfits and struggles with new categories. A new framework called ICARE aims to fix this. It has two parts. First, an instance selection step picks the best training examples to show the system. Second, knowledge distillation passes what the system already knows from one task to the next, covering both its internal features and its final decisions. The authors say tests on benchmark text classification datasets showed a significant gain in accuracy on target tasks and less forgetting. The source code is public.

items.headline: TETHER Uses Table of Contents to Map Long, Complex Documents
items.summary: Researchers have built TETHER, a method that helps AI understand the structure of long documents like sustainability reports, product manuals and annual reports. Many tools guess structure from how text looks, which fails when designs are fancy. Asking an AI model to extract it directly can lead to made-up results in long files. TETHER instead reads the table of contents first and builds an outline from it, using an image-and-text AI model. Then it matches each block of content to that outline. It needs no extra training. In tests on documents in several languages, it beat other parsers and AI models. The authors also report it uses 90% fewer tokens, the chunks of text an AI processes, and runs much faster than end-to-end approaches.

items.headline: Large Training Runs Show Which AI Designs Really Work, and Which Benchmarks Miss
items.summary: Researchers ran 64 training runs from scratch, using Transformers and three types of linear models, from 1.3 to 8 billion parameters. Some used up to 2 trillion tokens of text. At small scale, design differences nearly vanish. At large scale, they show up. Canon layers, which mix nearby tokens, helped Transformers and saved about 30% of training tokens for the same MMLU score at 8B. With Canon, the simplest linear model matched a more complex one and beat Mamba2. But standard benchmarks hid flaws: linear models could not reliably find information in a 500-token text, and no model beat random guessing on a simple two-step question. The authors suggest adding reasoning examples to training data early.

items.headline: PRKV Trims LLM Memory Use by Ranking Which Tokens Matter
items.summary: Large language models keep a memory of earlier text, called the KV cache, and it grows very large for long inputs. Researchers introduce PRKV, a method that decides which parts of this memory to throw away. It uses Personalized PageRank, a ranking idea from web search, on the model's attention patterns. This lets it spot tokens that matter indirectly, not just recent ones. It needs no extra training and does not change the model. Tests covered long-document understanding, sparse retrieval and step-by-step reasoning on several model families. Even when cutting memory by up to 90%, PRKV stayed competitive with existing methods, lowered peak memory use, and added little extra run time. The results suggest a good balance between accuracy and memory for long inputs.

items.headline: PsyWorld Predicts Human Behavior by Learning How People's States Change
items.summary: Researchers introduced PsyWorld, an AI model that predicts what a person will do next. Most personalized AI agents use a fixed personality profile to pick actions. PsyWorld also learns from how a person's situation and state actually changed over time. A "world model" is an AI that learns how conditions shift from one moment to the next. The team tested it in a behavior simulator called VEET, using 48 unseen test participants. It reached 0.904 Top-1 accuracy, meaning its first guess was right that share of the time. Tests removing parts of the model showed that predicting the next state drove most of the gain. The authors say the results do not prove real psychological causes, and do not show reliable long-term predictions.

items.headline: New Method Predicts and Fixes Clashes When Merging Fine-Tuned AI Models
items.summary: Model merging combines several AI models, each fine-tuned for a different task, into one by adding their changes to a shared base model. Tasks can interfere with each other, and people usually only find out after building and testing the merge. This paper shows that a simple measure of how one task's output shifts under another task's changes can predict this interference, but only when measured at the right point, the fine-tuned model itself rather than the original base. Using this, the authors build LR-Merge, which tunes merge settings using unlabeled data and no backpropagation through the merged network. It improved every base merging method they tested, with larger gains as more tasks were merged. It matches a costlier exact approach that took about three times longer to converge, and answers new queries in seconds.

items.headline: New Feedback Method Helps Sparse Image Attacks Hit Target Pixel Density
items.summary: Researchers study attacks that tweak only a small share of pixels in an image to test how robust AI models are. These attacks use a neural network that generates the changes. Today, the share of changed pixels is set by a fixed setting that is hard to predict and drifts during training, so it needs repeated re-tuning. The team proposes Density Feedback Control. After each training round, it checks how many pixels are changed and tightens or loosens that setting to match a target. At a 10% target, it kept three base attacks within one percentage point of the goal in a single run. For two of them, it also raised the success rate of attacks that transfer to other models, while changing fewer pixels. It gave no steady gain for a third attack that limits changes to important image regions.

items.headline: New Method Helps Language Models Give More Varied Answers
items.summary: Language models often write good single answers, but when asked for several, the answers tend to repeat the same idea. This paper offers a way to pick a set of answers that are both good and different from each other. The method, called PoolDPP, first generates a pool of candidate answers. It then favors higher-quality ones and uses a statistical tool called a determinantal point process to choose a set that avoids near-duplicates. The authors prove that the chosen set gets closer to the ideal one as the pool grows. In tests, it improved the balance of quality and variety in open-ended writing and in ambiguous text-to-SQL tasks. On math problems from GSM8K, it gave more varied answers while solving about as many problems.

items.headline: Study Tests Whether Trimming Data Features Helps AI Resist Attacks
items.summary: Attackers can trick machine learning models by feeding them bad or sneaky data. Feature reduction cuts the number of data columns a model uses, which can speed up training and reduce overfitting. But researchers say its effect on attack resistance is not well understood. This study tested four such methods on five common model types, including decision trees and random forests. It used three attack types: poisoning, backdoor, and universal adversarial perturbation, on the APT dataset. Two methods, permutation importance ranking and univariate mutual information, gave the most consistent gains in robustness. The other methods worked well in some cases and poorly in others, depending on the model and the attack.

items.headline: AI Search Reviews Gemini 4 Neon in Hands-On Video Tests
items.summary: YouTube channel AI Search has posted a review of a model it calls Gemini 4 Neon. The video runs through many tests. These include a live piano duel, reverse engineering visual effects, making educational animations, and composing music. It also tries building 3D characters and a game, working with Blender for VR, and spotting cancer in images. Later sections cover deep research, generating new ideas, usage, and cost and speed benchmarks. The description gives no results or scores, so how well the model did is not stated in the text. The video is sponsored by Luma, and the host also links reviews of other models.

items.headline: llm-gemini 0.38.1 adds missing top reasoning level for Gemini 4 models
items.summary: Simon Willison released a small update to llm-gemini, his plugin that lets the LLM tool use Google's Gemini models. Gemini 4 Carbon supports three reasoning levels: low, medium and high. Hydrogen and Neon also have a fourth level, called xhigh. Willison missed this when he first added those models, and the new release fixes it. The extra setting matters. In his comparison, Hydrogen at high used 5,311 output tokens and cost 3.99 cents. At xhigh it used 31,477 tokens and cost 23.61 cents. The pelican image it produced was competitive with the one from Gemini 4 Neon. So higher reasoning can improve results, but it costs more.

items.headline: Free trial abuse floods AI product ChatPRD, forcing founder to end trials
items.summary: Claire Vo runs ChatPRD, an AI tool that helps product managers turn an idea into a spec. In a new YouTube video, she describes a wave of "token fraud" from people abusing her free trial. Tokens are the units AI companies use to measure and charge for usage. Some users just wanted free AI. Others resold tokens or ran businesses on top of her agent. She says one group looped through free trials and promo codes to build Roblox and Fortnite maps. Many prompts asked for SVG drawings of pelicans riding bicycles, which may be a way to guess which AI model sits underneath. Vo is now ending free trials entirely.

items.headline: Hebbia reports better financial research results with GPT-6 Astra
items.summary: Hebbia, a company that builds tools for financial research, tested GPT-6 Astra, a new model from OpenAI, before its public release. In its early evaluations, Hebbia found improvements in three areas. The model covered more sources, picked more relevant citations (the references that back up a claim), and produced better-presented results. The source does not give specific numbers. Still, the results suggest the model could help analysts who need thorough, well-sourced answers when researching financial questions.

items.headline: OpenAI's MedChemBench tests if AI can spot promising drug candidates
items.summary: OpenAI has described a new test called MedChemBench. It checks how well AI models handle early steps in drug discovery. The test looks at three skills. First, can the model read molecular structures, which are the shapes and makeup of chemical compounds? Second, can it reason from experimental evidence? Third, can it pick which compounds to pursue? Early drug discovery is the stage where scientists narrow down many possible compounds to a few worth studying. The benchmark gives a way to measure whether AI could support that work. The source gives no results or scores.

items.headline: Hugging Face Welcomes Inkling 2 Mini for Local Setups
items.summary: Hugging Face has published a blog post welcoming a model called Inkling 2 Mini.
